hypothesis: The ETF panel is fit for systematic research after validation and an explicit missing-data policy, with no observation deleted.
notes: Zero blocking errors. All 20%+ moves corroborated by peer returns and volume, so retained. Known residual bias: the universe consists of ETFs that survive today (§7.5.2).

hypothesis: A 15-ETF multi-asset universe contains far fewer independent risk dimensions than it contains assets, and that number falls further in crises.
notes: PC1 (equity vs duration) and PC2 (rates level) dominate. Only a handful of eigenvalues clear the Marchenko-Pastur noise bound, so covariance shrinkage is justified before optimisation rather than after it disappoints.

parameters.pca_input: correlation matrix of daily total returns

hypothesis: Daily ETF returns are not normally distributed, so parametric VaR will understate the tail.
notes: Every asset rejects normality at any conventional level. Historical simulation is the default VaR method in Stage 9 as a direct result.

hypothesis: Does GARCH(1,1) materially improve volatility forecasts over simpler rolling and EWMA estimators? (spec §32)
notes: GARCH wins on QLIKE but a short-half-life EWMA wins on correlation and R^2 at a fraction of the complexity. EWMA is kept as the production estimator; GARCH is retained as a documented extension, not adopted.

hypothesis: vol scaled 126 momentum predicts subsequent 21-day cross-sectional ETF returns.
notes: IC +0.0122, p=0.7753: no evidence of predictive content. At the family level, 15 of 72 tests clear a naive 5% threshold against 3.6 expected by chance, and 10 survive Benjamini-Hochberg control with the hypothesised positive sign. Cross-sectional momentum across heterogeneous asset classes is a much weaker effect than the within-equity version the literature usually reports: the cross-section here is dominated by the volatility difference between bonds and commodities rather than by relative trend. The signal is carried forward to the backtest anyway, so that the portfolio-level result can be compared against this signal-level evidence rather than replacing it.

hypothesis: The 21-day price z-score is NEGATIVELY related to subsequent 5-day returns (mean-reversion hypothesis, beta < 0).
notes: IC +0.0089, p=0.6496: no evidence of predictive content. At the family level, 6 of 72 tests clear a naive 5% threshold against 3.6 expected by chance, and 5 survive Benjamini-Hochberg control with the hypothesised negative sign: zscore_ranked_5@h1, zscore_5@h1, zscore_10@h1, zscore_ranked_10@h1, reversal_5@h1. Every survivor sits at the 1-day horizon with a short lookback, so the effect is real but decays almost immediately. That decay profile, not the peak IC, sets the tradable holding period, and a 1-day holding period means transaction costs will decide whether any of it survives -- which Stage 6 tests directly.

hypothesis: Correcting for overlapping observations materially changes the evidence for both signal families, and the Fundamental Law implies only a modest information ratio even before costs.
notes: Naive standard errors understate uncertainty by up to 3.3x on overlapping forward returns. Both families' information is concentrated at 1-5 days, where the implied pre-cost information ratio is at its highest and the required turnover is also at its highest -- the central tension the backtest must resolve. Momentum and reversion signals are close to uncorrelated in the cross-section, which is the precondition for the strategy-level diversification tested in Stage 10.

hypothesis: M3_momentum generates positive risk-adjusted returns after realistic transaction costs.
notes: Turnover of 9.2x per year costs 57 bps annually at the 10 bps baseline, taking the Sharpe ratio from 0.38 gross to 0.30 net. The strategy breaks even at 27.8 bps. This is the direct consequence of Stage 5's finding that the predictive information sits at the 1-5 day horizon: the only way to harvest it is to trade constantly, and the trading costs more than the signal is worth.

hypothesis: M4_mean_reversion generates positive risk-adjusted returns after realistic transaction costs.
notes: Turnover of 22.4x per year costs 139 bps annually at the 10 bps baseline, taking the Sharpe ratio from -0.04 gross to -0.24 net. The strategy breaks even at -1.1 bps. This is the direct consequence of Stage 5's finding that the predictive information sits at the 1-5 day horizon: the only way to harvest it is to trade constantly, and the trading costs more than the signal is worth.

hypothesis: M5_momentum_plus_mr generates positive risk-adjusted returns after realistic transaction costs.
notes: Turnover of 18.4x per year costs 116 bps annually at the 10 bps baseline, taking the Sharpe ratio from 0.23 gross to 0.06 net. The strategy breaks even at 8.5 bps. This is the direct consequence of Stage 5's finding that the predictive information sits at the 1-5 day horizon: the only way to harvest it is to trade constantly, and the trading costs more than the signal is worth.

hypothesis: Sophisticated portfolio optimisation improves risk-adjusted returns over naive equal weighting.
notes: The best model on full-sample net Sharpe is M1_inverse_vol. The risk-based allocators, which use no expected returns at all, beat every book that requires estimating mu. The estimation-error experiment explains why: an unconstrained optimiser holds 3 of 15 assets with a 77% maximum weight, and a perturbation of mu worth 25% of its cross-sectional dispersion moves up to 92% of the book. This is a full-sample comparison and therefore in-sample; Stage 11 re-runs it walk-forward before any conclusion is drawn.

hypothesis: Which covariance and volatility estimators produce the most useful out-of-sample risk forecasts? (spec §33)
notes: EWMA forecasts risk most accurately; shrinkage's contribution is conditioning, cutting the condition number from 35609 to 9764. Those are different goods and the distinction matters: an optimiser inverts the covariance matrix, so it is hurt far more by an ill-conditioned matrix than by a slightly less accurate one. The production configuration therefore uses EWMA for position sizing and shrinkage for anything that gets inverted. GARCH(1,1) is retained as a documented extension only: its mean persistence of 0.993 implies volatility shocks that decay over months, and it is integrated for 2 of 15 assets.

hypothesis: The VaR model is validated out of sample: breaches arrive at the promised rate and are independent through time.
notes: Rejected, and this is the most useful negative result in the project. Every method fails at 99% -- historical simulation breaches 1.48% of days against 1% promised -- and every method fails the Christoffersen independence test at 95%: the breach count is roughly right but the breaches arrive in clusters, because an unconditional model cannot represent volatility clustering. The practical consequence is that a single VaR number is not a risk limit; it must be paired with CVaR (whose realised/predicted ratio is 1.03, well calibrated) and with the regime analysis.

hypothesis: Risk-based allocation survives the post-COVID inflation shock better than equity beta does (Ch. 19 closing case study).
notes: 2022 is the regime that breaks the equity/bond diversification these books rely on: both legs fell together, so risk-based allocation had nowhere to hide. The regime correlation table quantifies it directly.

hypothesis: Combining strategy return streams improves risk-adjusted performance beyond the best individual strategy (Ch. 22 §22.5).
notes: The return streams are weakly correlated on average (+0.24), so combining does raise the Sharpe ratio above the *average* component. Whether it beats the *best* component is the sterner test and the one reported here: 0.78 versus 0.87. Combination is not alchemy -- it cannot turn two strategies with no edge into one that has an edge, and Stage 6 established that the alpha strategies have no edge net of costs. What it does is reduce the variance of the total, which is worth having when the components are genuinely positive.

hypothesis: The backtest engine and every production strategy are free of look-ahead bias.
notes: Perturbing all post-split data leaves every pre-split weight bit-identical for the production strategies, while the deliberately broken control strategy (built from tomorrow's return) is caught at every split date and in both perturbation modes. A test that never fails proves nothing, which is why the control is part of the suite rather than a one-off check.

hypothesis: momentum performance is robust across its parameter family, not the product of one fortunate choice.
notes: 75% of the 24 parameter combinations produce a positive net Sharpe ratio, with a best of 0.30 against a median of 0.08. Verdict: plateau: results are broadly similar across parameters

hypothesis: mean_reversion performance is robust across its parameter family, not the product of one fortunate choice.
notes: 39% of the 18 parameter combinations produce a positive net Sharpe ratio, with a best of 0.21 against a median of -0.15. Verdict: spike: the best parameter is far above the median, treat as parameter mining

hypothesis: Out-of-sample walk-forward performance justifies the model ladder's added complexity.
notes: The best out-of-sample model is M1_inverse_vol at a Sharpe ratio of 0.84, with a block-bootstrap 90% interval of [0.41, 1.28]. The interval is what the headline number should be read against: a Sharpe ratio of 0.8 over twenty years still carries an interval wide enough to contain materially worse outcomes, and nothing in this project is precise enough to distinguish the top few models from one another.

hypothesis: Final model comparison: which step of the ladder actually improved risk-adjusted returns after costs? (spec §55-§56)
notes: M1_inverse_vol has the highest full-sample net Sharpe ratio at 0.87, against 0.70 for equal weight and 0.65 for SPY buy-and-hold. The improvement over the naive benchmark comes almost entirely from risk-based weighting, not from alpha: every model that requires estimating expected returns lands below the models that do not.
